Node types

Four shapes to know.

Trigger
Starts the run. No input, one output.
Action Node
Does the work — calls an app or transforms data.
Flow Node
Routes the run: branch, filter, loop or merge.
AI Agent
AI Agent Node
Reasons and calls tools. Needs a model below.

Action node

Then the work happens.

Once a trigger fires, action nodes carry the run. n8n sorts them into four kinds — by what each one reaches for.

Google Drive
Action in an app
Do something in an outside app — send a message, add a row.
Code in Python
Data transformation
Reshape the data the run carries: map, filter or compute.
HTTP Request
Core
Reach the plumbing directly — call any API, set a webhook.
Chat
Human review
Pause and let a person approve before the run continues.

Flow node

The run doesn’t go straight.

Flow nodes don’t change your data — they steer it. Watch the ports: this is the one family where more than one wire leaves the box.

Kept
Filter
Drops items that fail a condition. Only what’s kept moves on.
true
false
If
Splits the run in two — one branch true, one branch false.
done
loop
Loop Over Items
Runs a branch once per item, then carries on when done.
Input 1
Input 2
Merge
Brings separate branches back into a single stream.

Two more things

Files in, and a short memory.

Both are switches on nodes you have already built. Neither needs a credential.

Allow File Uploads
One toggle on the chat trigger. A paperclip appears in the chat box, and whatever the user attaches arrives as binary data the agent can read.
Simple Memory
One node on the agent’s Memory port. It keeps the last few turns of the conversation so a follow-up like “resolve this” still means something.
You will send the same follow-up twice — once without memory, once with — and watch the answer change.

Letting go of it

Publish it, and walk away.

Everything so far has run inside the editor. The chat pane at the bottom of the canvas is a test harness, not a product.

Two switches and a button
One toggle on the chat trigger lists the workflow in n8n’s Chat hub. One press of Publish gives it a production URL. That is the entire procedure.
Then it runs without you
Anyone you have shared it with can open it from the Chat hub and talk to it — file uploads, memory and both replies — with no canvas in sight.
Test runs still land on the canvas. Published runs happen elsewhere, and stay out of the editor unless you turn on saving executions.

Tidying up

And how to throw one away.

You will collect junk workflows fast. Deleting one is deliberately more awkward than you expect.

Archive first
There is no Delete in the menu of a workflow you can see. Archive is the only option, and it destroys nothing — it takes the row out of the list.
Then un-hide it and delete
Tick Show archived workflows in the filter to bring it back. The menu on an archived row is a different menu, and Delete is finally in it.
Awkward on purpose. A workflow somebody else is chatting with should be hard to delete by accident.
